result:
The rain came down in silver needles that afternoon, the kind that finds every gap in your collar and reminds you that skin is just a polite suggestion. I stood under the awning of the closed florist on Mercer Street watching water race along the gutters like it had somewhere urgent to be. A woman hurried past with a newspaper over her head, the ink bleeding into her fingers. She looked like someone who had once believed in perfect timing.

I’ve been thinking about belief lately. Not the loud, declarative kind that fits on bumper stickers, but the quiet, almost embarrassed variety that keeps us upright when the evidence suggests we should fold. My grandmother used to say that hope was a muscle. You either exercised it until it grew strong or it atrophied into something useless and painful. She died at ninety-one still believing her husband would walk through the door any minute even though he’d been gone for forty-three years. I used to think that was tragic. Now I’m not so sure.

There’s a peculiar dignity in stubborn optimism. It’s easy to be cynical. Cynicism costs nothing and explains everything. But belief? Real belief, the kind that survives mortgage payments and medical diagnoses and the slow realization that most of your childhood dreams were statistically improbable? That costs. It costs sleep. It costs relationships sometimes. It costs the comforting armor of being right about how broken everything is.

I walked down to the river after the rain eased. The city smelled like wet concrete and possibility. A tugboat pushed a barge upstream, its engine making that low, patient sound that always makes me feel like I should be working harder at something. Two kids were trying to skip stones across the brown water. One of them had the technique all wrong, throwing with his whole arm like he was angry at the river itself. The stones plopped straight down every time. His friend kept trying to correct him but the kid wasn’t having it. Some people have to learn their own way, even if it means watching a hundred stones sink.

I’ve been that kid. Still am, probably.

There’s a Japanese concept called *wabi-sabi* that I’ve been turning over in my mind like a smooth stone. It’s the beauty found in imperfection, the acceptance that nothing lasts, nothing is finished, and nothing is perfect. We spend so much energy trying to polish ourselves into something Instagram-ready that we miss the particular loveliness of being cracked. The Japanese would repair broken pottery with gold, making the fractures part of the object’s history rather than its shame. I wonder what our lives would look like if we treated our failures that way instead of hiding them in the basement like embarrassing relatives.

Last week I found an old notebook from when I was twenty-three. The handwriting was frantic, all sharp angles and underlined phrases. “I will never settle,” it said. “I will never become boring.” The arrogance of youth is almost charming until you realize you’re reading it with the eyes of someone who has, in fact, settled in several important ways and has discovered that boredom is sometimes just peace wearing a different outfit.

The truth is more complicated, as truths tend to be. I have settled, but I’ve also refused to settle. Both statements are true on different days, sometimes within the same hour. Human beings contain these contradictions the way rivers contain both trout and plastic bottles. The trick isn’t to resolve them. The trick is to stop being surprised by them.

A man walked by pushing a shopping cart full of what looked like every possession he owned, carefully arranged. He had a system. You could tell by how methodically everything was packed. There was a dignity to it that made me look away, not out of discomfort but out of respect. Some people are building cathedrals with whatever materials they can find. We should probably stop assuming we know which ones are beautiful.

I keep thinking about my friend Marcus who died last spring. He was the kind of person who would start sentences with “The thing about life is…” and then proceed to say something so obviously true that you’d feel stupid for not having articulated it yourself. His last coherent sentence to me was, “Don’t wait to be ready.” He said it while hooked up to more machines than seemed medically advisable, his voice thin as paper. I’ve been carrying that sentence around like a talisman. Don’t wait to be ready. Because readiness is mostly an illusion anyway. We’re never ready for love or grief or the moment when our parents start becoming fragile. We just show up with whatever we have and figure it out as we go.

The light was changing over the water, that particular gold that only happens in late afternoon when the sun decides to get theatrical. I thought about all the versions of myself that had stood in this same spot over the years. The angry twenty-year-old. The confused thirty-year-old. The one who thought he had it all figured out at thirty-five and was proven wrong by dinner time. They’re all still here somehow, layered inside me like tree rings. The trick is to stop treating them like mistakes and start treating them like evidence that I’ve been becoming something all along.

A dog ran past me chasing a squirrel with absolute conviction. The squirrel made it up a tree with that particular rodent arrogance that suggests they know something we don’t. The dog stood at the bottom barking like this was a personal betrayal. I envied them both their clarity of purpose.

I’ve been trying to write a novel for seven years. It’s terrible in all the ways that matter and perfect in the only way that counts: it exists. Every time I open the document I can hear my younger self whispering *this is it, this is the one that’s going to work.* And every time I close it again I can hear my older self saying *maybe not today but definitely tomorrow.* Between those two voices is where the work actually happens. In the tension. In the not-knowing. In the stubborn refusal to declare the project either doomed or destined.

The sun slipped behind the buildings and the gold turned to lavender. The city changed its clothes for evening. Somewhere nearby someone was playing saxophone, badly but with enthusiasm. The notes floated over the water like they had important business with the moon.

I started walking home.

The streets were filling with people who had somewhere to be. I moved among them like a fish swimming upstream, content to be going the wrong direction. My shoes were still wet from the rain. My notebook was filling up with fragments that might become something or might not. Either way felt like grace.

There’s a line from a poem I can’t quite remember that goes something like *we are all just trying to get home.* I think about that a lot. Not home as a physical place necessarily, though that matters too. But home as the place where you stop performing. Where your contradictions are not just tolerated but expected. Where someone looks at the gold in your fractures and calls it beautiful.

The saxophone player hit a note that was so wrong it circled back around to being exactly right. I smiled without meaning to. An old woman smiled back at me like we shared a secret. Maybe we did.

By the time I reached my building the streetlights had come on, those sodium orange sentinels that make everything look like memory. I stood outside for a long time, keys in my hand, listening to the city breathe. Somewhere above me a couple was arguing about whose turn it was to take out the trash. Their voices drifted down like tired birds. I thought about how love sounds different at different altitudes. How the same words can be weapons or prayers depending on who’s saying them and why.

I finally went inside.

My apartment was quiet in the way only empty rooms can be. I made tea I didn’t really want. Sat at my desk and opened the novel that isn’t a novel yet. The cursor blinked at me like it had been waiting. For a moment I felt the full weight of every word I hadn’t written yet. Then I remembered Marcus and his machines and his paper-thin voice.

Don’t wait to be ready.

So I started typing. Not because I had something brilliant to say but because the rain had stopped and the light had changed and a dog had chased a squirrel and a woman had smiled at me like we knew each other and somewhere in all of that was the shape of something true.

The words came slowly at first, then faster, like water finding its way through cracks in stone. I wrote about the rain and the river and the saxophone that couldn’t quite find the note but kept trying anyway. I wrote about my grandmother waiting for a ghost and the man with his carefully arranged shopping cart and the kid who couldn’t skip stones but refused to be taught.

I wrote until my hands hurt and the tea went cold.

When I finally stopped, the city outside my window had gone quiet. Even the arguing couple had made peace or at least gone to bed angry. The cursor kept blinking, patient as geology, waiting for whatever came next.

I closed the laptop but didn’t turn off the desk light. Some things deserve to stay illuminated even when you’re not looking directly at them.

Outside, it started raining again. I could hear it against the windows like gentle fingers asking to be let in. I thought about letting it. Thought about opening every window in the place and just letting the water have its way. Instead I made more tea and sat in the dark listening to it fall.

There are worse ways to spend a life than this. Listening. Writing badly. Believing in spite of evidence. Carrying other people’s sentences around like talismans. Learning, slowly and with considerable resistance, that being cracked might be the whole point.

The rain kept falling. The novel kept not being finished. My wet shoes sat by the door like faithful dogs waiting to go out again tomorrow.

I fell asleep at my desk and dreamed about skipping stones that somehow never sank. They just kept bouncing across the water forever, making perfect circles that never quite touched.

When I woke up, the dream was still with me, light as breath.

I started typing again.

(Word count: 1,023)
